strengths: Novel application of conformal prediction to learn early stopping criteria for exact MIP solving, with rigorous distribution-free probabilistic guarantees on solution quality
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 correctly establishes conformal calibration via exchangeability, and Theorems 5.1-5.2 provide sample-conditional concentration bounds
Substantial practical speedups: 60-95% solve time reduction on most problem families while maintaining ≥95% success rate at 0.1%-optimality
Well-motivated formulation clearly illustrated in Figure 1; the three-step pipeline (train, calibrate, deploy) is clean and practical
Comprehensive experiments across 6 diverse problem families and 2 solvers with detailed results and honest limitations discussion
Technically sound: the squashing function ensures valid predictions, weighted loss focuses on critical regions, and mathematical framework is rigorous
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (conformal prediction, neural network predictors) in straightforward manner; Theorems 5.1-5.2 apply standard concentration bounds
Problem-dependent effectiveness severely limits impact: GISP achieves only 8% speedup; paper lacks characterization of which problem structures benefit from early stopping or why
Predictor quality dependence not characterized: no analysis of prediction error rates, failure modes, or conditions for good performance; no comparison to simpler baselines
Insufficient ablation studies: missing sensitivity analyses for network architecture, calibration set size, weighting function, and discretization step; no per-instance analysis
Strong unexamined assumptions: equation 3.2 assumes theta and t uniquely identify algorithm state only on same hardware; weighting function (Eq. 5) with 1/y_theta(t) may cause numerical instability
Unexplained experimental results: OTS-medium shows CP_COPT with 78.6% success rate despite conformal calibration guaranteeing ~95%; discrepancy needs explanation
Limited distribution shift investigation: acknowledges distribution shift sensitivity but provides no empirical analysis of robustness to domain shift
Expensive training requirement: requires solving instances to completion, limiting applicability to problems already solvable; does not extend frontier of tractable instances
Missing critical analyses: no failure mode characterization, limited investigation of generalization across problem families, no computational cost analysis of predictor inference

strengths: Technically sound theoretical contributions: Theorems 4.1-5.3 rigorously establish probabilistic guarantees using conformal prediction, with clever handling of continuous time trajectories via rolling minimums and left-inverses
Novel application: First to apply conformal prediction for accelerating exact MIP solving while providing formal guarantees; distinct conceptual approach (early stopping vs. improving proof search)
Significant practical speedups: 60-95% solve time reduction on 5/6 benchmark families while maintaining 0.1%-optimality with 95% probability
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Six diverse problem families, two solvers, extensive appendices with sensitivity analyses, convergence curves, and ablation studies
Correctly handles multiple testing: The remark in Section 4.1 identifies and properly addresses the multiple testing problem through pre-calibrated thresholds
Well-presented paper: Clear motivation, logical development from problem to theory to experiments, honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Severe practical limitations on applicability: Requires solving hundreds of instances to completion beforehand to obtain optimal values and solver trajectories. This is computationally expensive and infeasible when optimal solutions are unknown a priori, limiting real-world deployment

Critical gap between theory and practice: No analysis of how predictor quality affects theoretical guarantees. Section 5.4 admits poor predictors yield no speedup, but robustness of conformal guarantees to predictor errors is not characterized

Incomplete cost accounting: Training time (~30 min/GPU), calibration overhead (100 instances), and callback evaluation costs not amortized into speedup metrics. Fair comparison should include total end-to-end cost
Inconsistent performance across problem families: GISP achieves only 8% speedup vs. 60-95% on others. Root cause and conditions for method applicability not thoroughly explained

Unhandled edge cases: Paper does not address solver behavior when hitting time/memory limits before convergence (violating Assumption 3.1), infeasible/unbounded instances, or robustness to solver configuration changes
Distribution-specific training: Method requires separate training/calibration for each problem family. Cannot transfer knowledge across problem classes, severely limiting scope and practical impact
